50.title: The well of eighty-four steps
50.hook: at Goindval, Guru Amar Das builds a step-well open to every caste
50.tomorrow: first the row, then the audience
50.howItsDone: Pilgrims visit the Baoli Sahib at Goindval, where many walk down the eighty-four steps reciting the Japji and bathing; the well is remembered as a place Guru Amar Das opened to people of every caste.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seva, an old man carrying water through the dark, mocked as homeless. Faithful in small things.

Imagine being thirsty next to a well full of clean water, and not being allowed to drink from it. Not because it's private property. Because of the family you were born into. For centuries across South Asia, caste decided things like that: who could draw water from which well, who could eat with whom, who could touch whose cup. The man who had carried water for twelve years in the dark was now the third Guru, Guru Amar Das. He settled at Goindval, on the banks of the river Beas. And there he began to dig. Not a normal well. Something grander, and open to everyone.
screen: `THIRSTY, NEXT TO A FULL WELL.` → `CASTE DECIDED WHO COULD DRINK.` → `GURU AMAR DAS BEGINS TO DIG.`

segments.voice: It's called a baoli: a step-well. Instead of lowering a bucket on a rope, you walk down a long staircase into the earth until you reach the water. Step-wells are found across South Asia, some of them wonderfully beautiful. The one at Goindval has eighty-four steps, and it's still there today. What made it different: Guru Amar Das opened it to everyone. Every caste, every family, walked down the same steps and drew from the same water. In a world where a shared well could be a scandal, that was a quiet revolution, built of brick and stone. It also turned Goindval into a center for the Sikhs, a place people traveled to, and the first great Sikh place of pilgrimage. Now the number. Eighty-four is significant in Indian thought: tradition spoke of eighty-four lakh, or eight point four million, forms of life a soul might pass through. Sikh tradition says that a person who recites Guru Nanak's Japji on each of the eighty-four steps, bathing at each, can be freed from that long round of births. Many pilgrims still do it, going down step by step. Sikhs hold that practice in different ways: some as a promise, some as a devotional discipline, some as a picture of the long way down to the water of life. But everyone agrees on the baoli's first lesson. The water at the bottom doesn't know anyone's caste. It's the same for all who walk down to it.

segments.voice: Pour a glass of water, hold it and look at it, then sip slowly, letting each sip sit before you swallow. Think of where it came from, a river, a reservoir, rain, and of someone, somewhere, who is thirsty right now. If you pray, you can give thanks for water as you finish the glass.
Baoli. A step-well; the one at Goindval has eighty-four steps, and Guru Amar Das opened it to every caste. Today's word.
Your line: water for all. Tomorrow, first the row, then the audience. Fifty days, and counting.

51.title: First the row, then the audience
51.hook: anyone who comes to see the Guru eats first in langar; tradition says the emperor Akbar sat on the floor too
51.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, langar is served to anyone who comes, seated together in rows on the floor, in pangat; the saying pehlan pangat, pichhon sangat is often quoted to explain why.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the baoli, eighty-four steps down to shared water. Water for all.

Meeting someone important usually works the same way. A waiting room, a line, a list, and someone at a desk deciding who goes first. The more important the visitor, the shorter the wait. At Goindval, visiting Guru Amar Das worked differently. Before anyone at all could sit with the Guru, they first had to sit on the floor in the langar, the community kitchen, in a row with everyone else, and eat. Farmers, merchants, beggars, priests. And one day, tradition says, the Mughal emperor himself came to Goindval: Akbar.
screen: `WAITING ROOMS AND GUEST LISTS.` → `AT GOINDVAL, EVERYONE EATS FIRST.` → `THEN THE EMPEROR ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Sikhs sum up the rule in a short Punjabi saying: pehlan pangat, pichhon sangat. First the row, then the gathering. The pangat is the row of people sitting side by side on the floor to eat; the sangat is the gathering around the Guru. The order matters. You don't get to the Guru until you've eaten as an equal with everyone else. Tradition says Akbar honored the rule. The emperor sat down on the floor in the row, among ordinary people, and ate the simple food of the kitchen before he met Guru Amar Das. Some tellings add that he was so moved he offered the Guru a grant of land, and the Guru declined it, saying the kitchen should be supported by the community's own work and giving, not by a king. Historians note that the visit comes to us through Sikh tradition, and the details vary. But the rule itself is still kept today. Yesterday it was water; today it's food. A shared meal says who counts as your equal, and in that world rules of rank and caste said who could sit and eat with whom. The pangat wipes that line out, on the floor, every day. Nobody sits at the head. Nobody gets a higher seat. The same food, from the same pot, served by volunteers. Guru Nanak had begun the langar, and Mata Khivi had kept it going. Guru Amar Das made it the doorway. Before you meet the Guru, you meet your neighbor, at eye level, on the floor.

segments.voice: Picture the row: faces side by side, all at the same height. At your next meal, sit where you usually don't, and let someone else be served first, or serve everyone yourself and sit down last. If you eat alone, eat on the floor or at a counter, somewhere without a head of the table.
Pangat. The row where everyone, even an emperor, sat on the floor at Goindval and ate as equals before meeting the Guru.
Your line: nobody sits at the head. Tomorrow, the preachers, women and men. Until tomorrow.

52.title: The preachers, women and men
52.hook: he sends out preachers to lead sangats, women among them, and speaks against the burning of widows
52.howItsDone: In Sikh practice any person, woman or man, may lead prayer, read from the Guru Granth Sahib or perform kirtan; Sikhs cite Guru Nanak's words on women and Guru Amar Das's teaching on sati as part of the Gurus' stand for women's equality.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pangat, the row, and an emperor on the floor at Goindval. Nobody sits at the head.

When something starts to grow, a small business, a club, a movement, there comes a moment when the founder can't be everywhere. People are joining in towns far away. They want to learn, and they can't all travel to one village by the river. That's where the Sikhs were by the time of Guru Amar Das, with communities across the Punjab and beyond. So the Guru did something practical. He chose trusted people and sent them out, each to look after a region, teach the hymns and gather the community. And tradition says some of those he trusted with this were women.
screen: `THE FOUNDER CAN'T BE EVERYWHERE.` → `COMMUNITIES ACROSS THE PUNJAB.` → `TRUSTED TEACHERS, SENT OUT.`

segments.voice: The word is manji. A manji is a simple cot, a low wooden frame strung with rope, the kind people sat on in Punjabi courtyards. The teacher sat on the manji, and the community gathered on the ground around it. So manji came to mean the teaching post itself: the seat, and the responsibility that went with it. Sikh tradition speaks of twenty-two manjis set up by Guru Amar Das, spreading the teaching across a wide region. And tradition says women were among those trusted to teach and lead. The Guru also spoke directly about women's lives. One practice of that time and place was sati, the burning of a widow on her husband's funeral fire. In a hymn in the scripture, Guru Amar Das redefines the word. A true sati, he says, is not a woman who burns herself on her husband's pyre; it's one who lives with goodness and contentment, and honors her beloved by how she lives. He's also remembered for discouraging the veil for women at the gathering, and for standing against the idea that a woman's worth ended with her husband's life. Behind it all is a line of Guru Nanak's that Sikhs quote often. Why call her lesser, he asks, from whom kings are born? We are born of woman, we are married to woman, it is through woman that the world goes on. To be honest, Sikh communities, like others, have lived up to this unevenly. But the Gurus' words are clear, and they're in the book.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one woman who taught you: a mother or grandmother, a teacher, a boss, an older sister, a neighbor, a friend, someone who sat, in a way, on a manji for you. Remember one thing she taught you, in words or without them. If she's alive, think how you'd tell her; if she's gone, just thank her, quietly.
Manji. A simple rope cot, and the teaching seat Guru Amar Das gave trusted women and men to lead communities. Today's word.

53.title: The song of bliss
53.hook: tradition links his great hymn, the Anand Sahib, to joy at a grandson's birth; it is sung at every ceremony
53.howItsDone: The Anand Sahib is part of the Sikh daily prayers, and its first five stanzas with the fortieth are sung at the close of congregational worship and at weddings, namings and funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: manji, a rope cot that became a teaching seat. Your line was she is not lesser.

Good news has a way of tumbling out before the hello is over. Mom, guess what. Guru Amar Das was an old man by now. Tradition says a grandson was born to his son, Mohri, and the family was full of joy. The baby was named Anand. Around that time, tradition says, the Guru composed a hymn Sikhs still sing at every turn of life. It opens, in effect, with that same rush of good news, told to a mother.
screen: `GOOD NEWS, TUMBLING OUT.` → `MOM, GUESS WHAT.` → `A GRANDSON, AND A HYMN.`

segments.voice: It's called the Anand Sahib, the song of bliss. Anand means bliss, deep joy, the kind that settles in rather than flashing past. The hymn has forty stanzas, in raga Ramkali. Its first line goes something like this, in paraphrase: I am in bliss, O my mother, for I have found my true Guru. Notice who hears the news first: mother, the one who has known the singer longest. And the news isn't wealth or success. The singer has found the true Guru, and the mind is at peace. The hymn says this bliss can't be bought or faked; it comes through the Guru's word, and it sings of the Word ringing inside like music. Tradition links the hymn to the grandson's birth, and the child and the hymn share a name. You may have heard it without knowing. The Anand Sahib, or its opening stanzas and last stanza, is sung at Sikh ceremonies of every kind: a wedding, a baby's naming, the end of the congregation's prayers, even a funeral. Joy, on this path, isn't only for happy days. It's the steady bliss of being close to the Guru, and it holds even when life is sad. Those same stanzas are part of Rehras, the Sikh evening prayer. A song that began with a family's joy now closes Sikh gatherings.

segments.voice: Sing or hum something joyful: a lullaby, a hymn from your childhood, a song from a wedding you loved. Nobody's listening, and it doesn't have to be good; let your chest buzz with it. If gladness comes, let it stay a moment, and if it doesn't, just keep the tune going.

54.title: Jetha the orphan
54.hook: an orphaned boy selling boiled grams at Lahore comes to Goindval, serves, and marries Bibi Bhani
54.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Ram Das, born Jetha, as the fourth Guru, and tell his orphaned childhood and years of service as a sign that the Gurus chose by devotion, not birth; Bibi Bhani is honored as a pillar of the early community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand, the song of bliss, first told to a mother. Your line was bliss, mother, bliss.

A crowded market street in Lahore. Carts, dust, shouting. A small boy with a tray calls out to passersby: boiled grams, hot boiled grams. Chickpeas, cooked and salted, a street snack that costs next to nothing. His name is Jetha. His parents have both died. He's about seven, tradition says, selling snacks on the street to help keep himself alive. This Guru's story begins with almost nothing at all.
screen: `A MARKET STREET IN LAHORE.` → `HOT BOILED GRAMS.` → `A BOY NAMED JETHA, ORPHANED.`

segments.voice: Jetha went to live with his grandmother in Basarke, the very village Guru Amar Das came from. So when pilgrims set out from there to see the Guru at Goindval, the young man went with them. And he stayed. He did what Amar Das had once done for Guru Angad: he served. Tradition says he carried baskets of earth for the step-well, worked in the kitchen, went wherever a pair of hands was needed. No money, no family connections. Just his work. And someone noticed. The Guru's wife was looking for a husband for their daughter, Bibi Bhani. Tradition says she saw Jetha working and said: a young man like that. The Guru agreed. The orphan who once sold grams on the street married the Guru's daughter. Bibi Bhani is honored in her own right, remembered for her devoted service to her father. She would become the wife of one Guru, the mother of another, and the grandmother of a third. Jetha kept serving, for years. Eventually Guru Amar Das chose him as his successor, and he became the fourth Guru, Guru Ram Das. Notice the baskets: Jetha carried earth for a step-well open to every caste, and the boy with nothing became family to the Guru. Sikhs tell it to say that nobody's beginning is too small. The Gurus looked at who people could become, not where they started.

55.title: The pool of nectar
55.hook: Guru Ram Das begins the pool and the town that will be named Amritsar, the pool of nectar
55.howItsDone: Amritsar is the spiritual center of the Sikh world; pilgrims bathe in the sacred pool and walk around it, and many volunteer in its seva, cleaning the tank and serving in the langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jetha, from a tray of boiled grams to the fourth Guru. Your line was small beginnings.

Most towns grow up around something. A crossroads, a harbor, a mine, a railway station. Take away the thing in the middle and the town stops making sense. Today, the beginning of a city millions visit every year, one of the most famous in the world for Sikhs. It didn't grow up around a market or a fort. Before it was a city, it was a patch of land with a small natural pond, surrounded by trees. Guru Amar Das, tradition says, asked Jetha, now his son-in-law, to find a place for a new center. And Guru Ram Das began to dig.
screen: `EVERY TOWN GROWS AROUND SOMETHING.` → `A SMALL POND, AND TREES.` → `GURU RAM DAS BEGINS TO DIG.`

segments.voice: The city is Amritsar. Amrit means nectar, the water of immortality, and sar means pool: the pool of nectar. At first the settlement was called Guru ka Chak, the Guru's village, and later Ramdaspur, after Guru Ram Das. The name Amritsar came from the pool itself. Tradition says the Guru had the pond dug out and widened into a great tank, a sacred pool. Sikhs came to help, carrying earth in baskets on their heads, the same work Jetha once did at the step-well. Here's the practical genius. The Guru didn't only build a place of worship. He invited people to come and live there: traders and craftsmen of many kinds, tradition says, so the town would have its own markets and its own living. Worship and work, side by side; Kartarpur again, on a bigger scale. Sikhs tell a story about the pool, too. A young woman named Rajni, married off by her angry father to a man with leprosy, is said to have left her husband by the water while she went for food. He saw a crow dip into the pool and come out white, bathed himself, and was healed. It's a story people tell, and the tree by that spot is still honored. Guru Ram Das didn't live to see the pool finished; that would fall to his son. But he gave the town its center, and the thing in the middle was a pool of still water.

56.title: The four rounds
56.hook: he writes the four lavan, the wedding hymns that Sikh couples still walk around the Granth to (Suhi, ang 773)
56.howItsDone: In the Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding, the couple walks four times clockwise around the Guru Granth Sahib as each of Guru Ram Das's four lavan is read and then sung, joined by a scarf.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amritsar, the pool of nectar. Your line was a town around a pool.

If you've been to a Sikh wedding, you've seen it. Morning, in the gurdwara. The couple sits before the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture, on its raised seat. The bride holds one end of a long scarf, the groom the other. The musicians begin to sing, and the couple stands and walks slowly around the scripture, clockwise, the groom a step ahead, the scarf between them. They sit. The singing starts again. They walk again. Four times in all. Every round is a hymn, and all four were written by the orphan from Lahore, Guru Ram Das.
screen: `A MORNING WEDDING IN THE GURDWARA.` → `A SCARF BETWEEN THEM.` → `FOUR WALKS AROUND THE SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: They're called the lavan, the rounds. The hymn is in the scripture, in raga Suhi, with four stanzas, one for each round. Each describes a stage, in paraphrase. The first: the duties of a good life, following the Guru's teaching, living honestly, remembering God's name. The second: meeting the true Guru; fear falls away, and the mind is humbled. The third: the heart fills with longing and love, detached from the world's pull. The fourth: the mind is at peace, and the soul and God are united as one. Sikhs hear the lavan as two marriages at once. On the surface, a husband and wife walking into a shared life. Underneath, the soul's marriage to God, the union the hymn keeps singing toward. So the couple isn't only promising themselves to each other; together they walk the soul's path, round by round, with the scripture at the center. The wedding is called the Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss. Remember Anand? It's usually closed with the Anand Sahib. Now look back over the week. The baoli, water for all. The row, even for an emperor. The manji, and she is not lesser. Anand, the song of bliss. Jetha the orphan. Amritsar, the pool. And now four rounds, one life. Two Gurus, one idea running through them: everyone at the same level, walking the same path, with the Word in the middle.
screen: `LAVAN — FOUR ROUNDS, FOUR STANZAS.` · `DUTY, THE GURU, LOVE, UNION.` · `TWO MARRIAGES AT ONCE.` · `THE ANAND KARAJ, CEREMONY OF BLISS.` · then, large: `FOUR ROUNDS, ONE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Think of a promise you keep, not one you've broken: to a partner, a child, a friend, a parent, yourself. Remember when you made it, and every time since that you've kept it, round after round. If you pray, give thanks for it; if not, just feel how long you've carried it.
Lavan. The four rounds of the Sikh wedding: four stanzas by Guru Ram Das, sung as the couple walks around the scripture. Today's word.
